summary: For ages 7–9, learners gather, record, classify, and present real data using tables, bar charts/pictograms, labelled diagrams, and classification keys. The core skill is construction and format-selection: building a display that actually answers the original question, and building a key as a chain of yes/no questions about observable features, each of which must split the group. Pupils both use and build keys. Reading and choosing displays can be assessed separately, and a static exemplar chart can serve as a reference scaffold, while the primary objective remains constructing displays, not only recognising them.
misconceptions: Always defaulting to a bar chart regardless of whether the data suits it, or drawing a bar chart of individual items rather than category totals.
Omitting headings, labels or a key, making the display unreadable to anyone else.
Building a classification key with questions that don't cleanly split the group (overlapping or non-observable criteria).
Confusing classifying (grouping by feature) with simply listing.
Treating the chart as the finished goal rather than as a tool that answers the original question.

activities.title: Data studio: build the table, then pick the display that reveals the answer
steps: Start from a real question and a pile of collected data, e.g. minibeasts found in the playground, or favourite-fruit votes.
Enter the collected values into a table and decide the column headings before entering data — one kind of information per column (e.g. category | count).
Generate a bar chart or pictogram from the table and toggle between formats.

Deliberately try a poor format first: a bar for every single individual item makes an unreadable 'forest'; then switch to category totals so the tallest bar answers 'which is most common?' at a glance.
Check that two categories with the same count produce bars that look the same size, and that a pictogram uses one symbol = one fixed amount with equal intervals.
Add axis labels, a scale/key, and table headings so a stranger could read the display without you explaining it.
activities.insight: Choosing the RIGHT representation is what makes data answer the question; a table holds exact values, a bar chart compares category totals, and labels/headings/scale are what make the display readable by someone else.

activities.title: Key-builder: sort creatures with yes/no feature questions
steps: Take the same set of organisms and place a chain of yes/no questions about observable features, e.g. 'Does it have wings?', 'Does it have six legs?'
Watch the creatures funnel down the branches of the key until each one ends up alone or in a correctly sorted group.
If a question fails to split the group, notice that some creatures get stuck together — revise the question so every step divides the group.
Also practise USING a given key to identify an unknown organism, following the yes/no path.
Present the sorted groups as a labelled diagram or simple key, and state for each group the observable feature that defines it, so someone else could sort a new specimen the same way.
activities.insight: A classification key is a chain of splitting questions; every question must cleanly divide the group, and groups must be defined by features you can see — not by feelings or opinions.

activities.title: Choose and read the display (reading-side check)
steps: Answer 'which chart best shows this data?' given a question and a dataset, and justify the choice (table for exact values, bar chart to compare categories, key to sort by features).
Use a given classification key to identify an organism by following the yes/no path.
Sort a set of data entries into the correct columns of a headed table.
Explain what each column of a table tells a reader, and whether equal counts appear as equal bars.
activities.insight: Being able to match data to an appropriate format and read charts/keys accurately is a distinct, checkable skill that complements building displays.

activities.title: Reference: anatomy of a good chart and key (scaffold)
steps: Study a labelled exemplar bar chart and classification key, revealing the parts: headings, labelled axes, even scale/consistent symbol value, and yes/no branch questions.
Use the exemplar as a checklist when building your own table, chart, or key.
activities.insight: A well-made display has identifiable parts — headings, labels, an even scale, and cleanly splitting questions — that you can check your own work against.

checkQuestion: Here are the minibeasts we found in the playground and what we noticed about each one. Organise this into a clear table, make a bar chart or pictogram showing how many of each we found, and sort them into groups using a labelled diagram or a simple key. (Provide the raw observations and materials; watch how the child organises, charts, and groups.)
checkAnswer: The child organises the observations into a table with appropriate column headings, builds a bar chart or pictogram with equal intervals and a consistent key/scale that shows the counts, and sorts the minibeasts into groups defined by observable features (e.g. number of legs, wings/no wings), presented as a labelled diagram or simple yes/no key.
